newsitem.title: UK: Reinsurers face hard line at Baden-Baden - industry.
newsitem.headline: Reinsurers face hard line at Baden-Baden - industry.

text.p: Reinsurers expect to encounter considerable pressure to cut rates for the 1997 renewals season at next week's industry meeting in Baden-Baden, southern Germany.
"We are expecting conversations to be about reductions in rates in just about all classes of business," one reinsurer told Reuters.

"It's going to be a very difficult renewal season. Prices are down all over the world," said another. The Baden-Baden meeting signals the start of the annual round of talks ahead of reinsurance renewals in January.
The current soft market follows three profitable years for most reinsurers which have led insurers to adopt an aggressive stance when negotiating reinsurance cover.
Insurers point out that during this period reinsurers' premium income has, in most cases, far outweighed claims payments and there is no sign of the situation changing.
"We will be looking for rate reductions if the weather stays calm. Much depends on the next few months," one reinsurance buyer at a leading European insurer said.
Baden-Baden plays host to one of the largest annual gatherings of reinsurers in the world. The meeting runs from Monday, October 21 to Friday, October 25.
Upwards of 850 representatives from 300 insurance and reinsurance companies are expected to attend the industry's 16th annual meeting in the spa town.

Europeans will account for around 80 percent, the largest contingents coming from Germany and the UK, but there will also be many from the Middle East, Asia, America and Australia, with 40 countries represented in total.
Companies from eastern Europe and China will be more strongly represented than in previous years.
Pressure for cuts in reinsurance rates was apparent at last month's insurance industry gathering in Monte Carlo, but it is only in Baden-Baden that serious negotiations will begin.
Reinsurers concede that in Europe at least they have seen three good years, with no catastrophes and few large, single loss events. "Buyers will expect some good news," said one reinsurer.
Reinsurers say they need five good years to offset the bad ones, adding that after three years they are only at break-even, but they realise that market forces are not in their favour.
"We've had over-capacity and good results in recent years. The two combined are a good indicator that things are going to get tougher," one reinsurer said.
Some reinsurance programmes renewed during the current year have seen rate reductions of 30 percent or more.
"Reductions of 30 percent are not uncommon. I've seen some even higher," said another reinsurance source.

With little impetus in the form of large claims to support the argument for maintained or higher rates, some fear a competitive drive for market share at the expense of the bottom line when disasters and catastrophes make their inevitable comeback.
"This is a very weak market and many reinsurers are fighting to keep market share. They're determined to fight on price," said one industry source.
"We're not interested in following prices down, but some haven't been around as long as we have and don't have the history."

Apart from rating levels, insurers said they would also be interested in discussing the possible effects of an unprecedented wave of major acquisitions in the global reinsurance market in recent months.
Some insurers said that in the wake of this consolidation they might need to reconsider their reinsurance programmes to ensure they are not concentrated among too few companies.
-- John Sanders, Reuters Insurance News 44 171 542 2769
